title: Something Big Has Happened: why emotionally engineered content wins on X and how to resist it
summary: Rob Hallam dissects a viral 65M-view AI post as emotional engineering, showing how X's algorithm rewards fear, urgency and long native text. He argues viral reach reflects emotion, not accuracy, and gives habits for resisting manufactured urgency while still using AI as a tool.

principles.text: Platform algorithms reward emotional activation, not accuracy, so emotional content outruns nuanced content.
principles.quote: The algorithm doesn't ask: is this accurate? It asks: does this make people feel something strongly enough to engage?

principles.text: Content designed to go viral anchors a new idea to an existing strong feeling so the feeling transfers automatically.
principles.quote: anchor your new idea to an existing strong feeling, and the feeling transfers automatically.

principles.text: Native, long text posts that keep users on-platform get boosted; external links get suppressed. Format fits the algorithm.
principles.quote: Content that keeps you on the platform for more than two minutes gets a significant algorithmic boost. Posts that drive you to another website get suppressed.

principles.text: Manufactured urgency is a sign to pause: wait 24 hours before sharing because real information rarely expires that fast.
principles.quote: If something makes you feel an urgent need to share it immediately, that urgency is almost certainly manufactured. Real information rarely expires in 24 hours.

principles.text: Check incentives: when a persuader ends with a call to action that benefits them, the content is a funnel.
principles.quote: The CEO of an AI company telling you to be afraid of AI and then selling you the solution is not a public service announcement. It's a funnel.

principles.text: Use AI as a tool but keep thinking; the winners decide clearly what to outsource and what to keep.
principles.quote: The people who will thrive are not the ones who outsource the most. They're the ones who think the most clearly about what to outsource and what to keep.
